The browser hangs for ages on load and sometimes the tab just dies. I've already tried minifying the JSON. What now?

A 180 MB GeoJSON with 400 k polygons is far beyond what a browser can chew in one go. The only realistic way to make it usable is **to stop sending the whole file to the client** and instead deliver **small, pre-processed chunks** (tiles) that are already simplified and optionally encoded in a more compact binary format.
Below is a practical, step-by-step roadmap you can follow right now, plus a few “quick-win” tricks you can try while you’re working on the longer-term tiling pipeline.

column3: What it means for your file
180 MB JSON → ~300 MB+ in memory after parsing (objects, strings, arrays)
column4: > 1 GB RAM, GC thrashing, UI freeze

column3: 400 k polygons → millions of vertices
`JSON.parse()` must allocate a huge object graph
Each vertex becomes a DOM/GL vertex
column4: Frame-rate drops to 0 fps, tab may be killed

column1: Even if you minify the file, you haven’t changed any of the above. You need to **reduce the amount of data the browser ever sees**.
## 2. Quick-win “client-side” tricks (useful while you build a proper tiling solution)

column3: How to do it
Serve the file with `Content-Encoding: gzip` (or `br`). Most browsers will automatically decompress.
column4: Reduces network transfer (180 MB → ~30-50 MB). Still too big for parsing, but at least the download is faster.

column3: Off-load `JSON.parse` to a Worker, then post the parsed object back (or stream chunks).
column4: Prevents UI freeze while parsing, but memory usage stays huge.

column3: Use a streaming JSON parser (e.g., `jsonparse`, `clarinet`, `oboe.js`) to read features one-by-one and feed them into a spatial index.
column4: Allows you to discard features you don’t need (e.g., outside the current viewport).

column3: Run `turf.simplify` (or `simplify-js`) on each feature as it streams in, with a tolerance that keeps visual fidelity.
column4: Cuts vertex count dramatically (often 70-90 % reduction) but still heavy if you keep all features.

column3: `topojson` removes duplicate coordinate sequences.
column4: Can shrink a 180 MB GeoJSON to ~70-80 MB, but you still need to decode it client-side.

column3: Use Mapbox GL JS / MapLibre GL, deck.gl, or Cesium to draw vertices on the GPU instead of Canvas/SVG.
column4: Improves frame-rate, but you still need to feed the GPU a manageable number of vertices (≤ few hundred k).

column1: > **Bottom line:** These tricks can buy you a few seconds of usability, but they won’t make a 180 MB file *smooth* on any typical desktop or mobile device. The real solution is **tiling**.
## 3. The “right” way: Serve the data as **vector tiles** (or another tiled binary format)

A vector tile is a small, fixed-size (usually 256 × 256 px) packet that contains **only the features that intersect that tile’s bounding box**, already **simplified** to the appropriate level of detail. The most common format is **Mapbox Vector Tile (MVT)**, a protobuf-encoded binary that is 10-100× smaller than raw GeoJSON.

column3: Why it matters for your 400 k polygons
A typical tile is 5-30 KB (compressed). Even a whole country can be served with a few hundred tiles.
Tiles are fetched on demand (only the viewport + a few surrounding tiles).
Lower-zoom tiles are heavily simplified; higher-zoom tiles contain more detail.
MVT is designed for WebGL renderers (Mapbox GL, MapLibre GL, deck.gl).
Tiles are cacheable by CDN, ETag, etc.
Server can generate tiles on-the-fly or pre-generate them once and serve static files.

### 3.4 If you can’t pre-generate tiles (dynamic data)

column3: How it works

Use **PostGIS + pg_tileserv**, **GeoServer** (MVT output), or **TileStache**. The server runs a spatial query (`ST_Intersects`) for each tile request, simplifies on the fly (`ST_SimplifyPreserveTopology`).
`geojson-vt` (Node.js) can generate vector-tile-like JSON tiles in memory. Combine with a simple Express endpoint: `GET /tiles/:z/:x/:y.json`.
Mapbox Tilesets, Amazon Location Service, Azure Maps, or Google Maps Platform can host your dataset and serve vector tiles without you managing a server.

### 3.4. Create the **layer views** that Tippecanoe will read

Tippecanoe works best with **GeoJSON** files, but it can also read from a PostgreSQL query via `ogr2ogr` or `psql` → `COPY`. The cleanest approach is to expose **materialised views** that already contain the exact columns you want, then dump each view to a temporary GeoJSON.
ST_Simplify(geom, 0.5) AS geom   -- 0.5 m simplification for zoom ≥ 12
CREATE INDEX idx_vw_roads_geom ON vw_roads USING GIST (geom);
WHERE water IS NOT NULL OR waterway IS NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX idx_vw_water_geom ON vw_water USING GIST (geom);
CREATE INDEX idx_vw_labels_geom ON vw_labels USING GIST (geom);
CREATE INDEX idx_vw_zones_geom ON vw_zones USING GIST (geom);
> **Why materialised?** They are static for a given release, so the view is computed once (`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`) and then read extremely fast by Tippecanoe.
### 3.5. Export each view to GeoJSON (one-off, then feed Tippecanoe)
> **Tip:** If you have > 5 M features, consider splitting the export per zoom level (see Tippecanoe `--maximum-zoom`/`--minimum-zoom` flags) to keep memory low.
